cards.front: An allele is one {{c1::version}} of a gene.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: What is the difference between a homozygous and a heterozygous organism?
cards.back: A homozygous organism has two of the same allele. A heterozygous organism has two different alleles.
cards.quote: A homozygous organism has two of the same allele, and a heterozygous organism has two different alleles.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: Your genotype is your pair of alleles, and your {{c1::phenotype}} is the trait that shows.
cards.quote: Your genotype is your pair of alleles, and your phenotype is the trait that shows.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In snapdragon flower color, why are both the red allele (R) and the white allele (W) written as capital letters?
cards.back: Neither symbol should suggest that one allele hides the other.
cards.quote: Both are capitals, so neither symbol suggests that one hides the other.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: {{c1::Incomplete dominance}} means the heterozygote shows a phenotype in between the two homozygotes, as in pink RW snapdragons.
cards.quote: Incomplete dominance means the heterozygote shows a phenotype in between the two homozygotes, as in pink RW snapdragons.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: A pink snapdragon looks like red and white paint mixed. Why is that picture misleading about the alleles?
cards.back: Paint stays mixed, but alleles do not. A pink RW plant still passes a separate R or W to each sex cell.
cards.quote: A pink plant still passes a separate R or W to each sex cell.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: {{c1::Codominance}} means the heterozygote shows the effects of both alleles.
cards.quote: Codominance means the heterozygote shows the effects of both alleles.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In Shorthorn cattle, what does an RW calf look like, and which kind of dominance is this?
cards.back: It is roan, with red and white hairs side by side. This is codominance.
cards.quote: so the first film switched to roan Shorthorn cattle
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In snapdragons, a pink RW plant is crossed with a white WW plant. Which colors should appear, and in what ratio?
cards.back: Pink and white offspring, about 1:1 on average. The pink parent passes R or W; the white parent passes only W, giving RW and WW.
cards.quote: The pink parent passes R or W; the white parent passes W.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: Two pink snapdragons (RW × RW) are crossed and 200 offspring are grown. How many red, pink and white plants are expected on average?
cards.back: About 50 red, 100 pink and 50 white. The square gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW, so the shares are 25%, 50% and 25% of 200.
cards.quote: genotype ratio 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW, and phenotype ratio 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: How do incomplete dominance and codominance differ in the heterozygote, and what do they share?
cards.back: Incomplete dominance gives an in-between phenotype; codominance shows the effects of both alleles. In both, the alleles stay separate and return in the next generation.
cards.quote: in both, the alleles stay separate and return in the next generation.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: A population can have more than two versions of a gene. How many alleles can one person carry?
cards.back: Only two, even when the population has more versions.
cards.quote: a population can have more than two versions of a gene, although each person carries only two.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: Which three common alleles make up the ABO gene in the usual model?
cards.back: IA, IB and i.
cards.quote: The ABO gene has three common alleles, IA, IB and i.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In the usual ABO model, which genotypes give type A blood, and what rule explains why?
cards.back: IA IA or IA i. IA is dominant to i, so one IA is enough to show marker A.
cards.quote: IA and IB are codominant, and each is dominant to i.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In the usual ABO model, one parent is type AB and the other is type O. Which blood types can their children have?
cards.back: Type A or type B, about half of each. The AB parent passes IA or IB, and the O parent passes only i.
cards.quote: The AB parent passes IA or IB; the O parent passes i.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In the usual ABO model, a type A parent (IA i) and a type B parent (IB i) have a child. Can the child be type O, and if so, how likely is it?
cards.back: Yes, about 1 in 4. Type O is ii, so the child must get i from each parent, which happens in one of four equally likely pairings.
cards.quote: IA and IB are codominant, and each is dominant to i.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: Two bigleaf hydrangea cuttings are genetically matched but grow in soils of different acidity. Must their flowers be the same color?
cards.back: No. The environment can change a phenotype. In many bigleaf hydrangeas, flowers are bluer in acidic soil and pinker in less acidic soil.
cards.quote: In many bigleaf hydrangeas, the same plant has bluer flowers in acidic soil and pinker flowers in less acidic soil.
cards.section: Explain: when neither allele hides the other

cards.front: In a standard pedigree, which shape stands for a male and which for a female?
cards.back: A square is a male and a circle is a female.
cards.quote: A square is a male, and a circle is a female.
cards.section: Explain: reading a family pedigree

cards.front: In a pedigree, two unshaded parents have a shaded child. If the trait is autosomal recessive, what must be true of each parent?
cards.back: Each parent must be a carrier: a heterozygote with a recessive allele who does not show the trait. The child needs two recessive copies, one from each parent.
cards.quote: In the recessive clue, each unshaded parent of a shaded child must be a carrier, a heterozygote who carries a recessive allele but does not show the trait.
cards.section: Explain: reading a family pedigree

cards.front: A pedigree shows a shaded child of two unshaded parents. A recessive model fits. Could a dominant model still explain it, and what does this say about pedigree conclusions?
cards.back: Possibly, if a new change in DNA started the dominant trait in this child. So the pedigree is a clue that favors recessive, not a proof.
cards.quote: Once in a while, though, a new change in DNA starts a dominant trait in a family with no history of it.
cards.section: Explain: reading a family pedigree

cards.front: Why can a pedigree not prove whether a trait is dominant or recessive?
cards.back: Its clues are only evidence for a model, and a small family may fit both models.
cards.quote: These are clues, not proofs. A small family may fit both models.
cards.section: Explain: reading a family pedigree

cards.front: A {{c1::karyotype}} is a picture of a cell's chromosomes sorted into matched pairs by size and shape.
cards.quote: A karyotype is a picture of a cell's chromosomes sorted into matched pairs by size and shape.
cards.section: Explain: a karyotype counts whole chromosomes

cards.front: How many chromosomes does a typical human body cell with a nucleus have, and how are they grouped?
cards.back: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes, usually XX or XY.
cards.quote: A typical human body cell with a nucleus has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes, usually XX or XY.
cards.section: Explain: a karyotype counts whole chromosomes

cards.front: A karyotype shows one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome. How many chromosomes does that cell have, and how is it written?
cards.back: 45 chromosomes, written 45,X. This pattern is linked to Turner syndrome. The 22 autosome pairs plus one X give 45.
cards.quote: It has 45 chromosomes, written 45,X.
cards.section: Explain: a karyotype counts whole chromosomes

cards.front: A cell has three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two, and nothing else is changed. How many chromosomes does it have, and what is this called?
cards.back: 47 chromosomes (46 plus one extra). It is called trisomy 21, the most frequent cause of Down syndrome.
cards.quote: Having three copies of chromosome 21, instead of two, is called trisomy 21.
cards.section: Explain: a karyotype counts whole chromosomes

cards.front: A cross, a pedigree and a karyotype each reveal a different scale of genetics. What does each one show?
cards.back: A cross shows allele pairings, a pedigree tests models across a family, and a karyotype counts whole chromosomes. A karyotype cannot show which alleles a person carries.
cards.quote: a cross shows allele pairings, a pedigree tests models across a family, and a karyotype counts whole chromosomes.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Nearly every body cell with a nucleus carries the same genes. Why do skin cells and muscle cells still differ?
cards.back: They express, or use, different sets of those genes.
cards.quote: skin and muscle cells differ because they use, or express, different sets of them.
cards.section: Explain: a karyotype counts whole chromosomes

cards.front: A pink × pink snapdragon cross is predicted to give 25% red, 50% pink, 25% white. Among U.S. blood donors, 48.8% were type O. Which number is a model prediction, which is measured, and which could change in a different group?
cards.back: The snapdragon shares are expected by the model. The 48.8% is measured and depends on the sample, so another group could differ. Type O is recessive (ii) in the usual model yet was most common.
cards.quote: Rows 4 to 7 depend on the sample; rows 1 to 3 are model predictions.
cards.section: Elaborate: model predictions and real blood-type counts

cards.front: A breeder asks whether pink snapdragons are heterozygotes (RW) or a third true-breeding color. What results from pink × pink and pink × white crosses would tell the ideas apart?
cards.back: If pink is RW, pink × pink gives about 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, and pink × white about 1 pink : 1 white. If pink is true-breeding, pink × pink gives only pink.
cards.quote: If pink is RW, pink × pink should give about 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, and pink × white about 1 pink : 1 white.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a snapdragon breeding experiment, why are pollen-making parts removed before they ripen and the flower covered after pollinating?
cards.back: So only pollen from the chosen parent reaches the flower and insects cannot bring other pollen. This keeps the cross controlled.
cards.quote: remove each flower's pollen-making parts before they ripen, brush on pollen from the chosen parent, and cover the flower so insects cannot bring other pollen.
cards.section: Design problem
